headline: UK and EU agree post-Brexit reset package at Brussels summit, with youth scheme, carbon market link and food rules still to be finalised

terms.meaning: The EU's shared trading area, where goods move with few checks or taxes.
A deal on food, plant and animal health rules so fewer border checks are needed.
A system that puts a price on carbon pollution; linking schemes lets each side recognise the other's permits.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree post-Brexit reset package at Brussels summit, with youth scheme, carbon market link and food rules still to be finalised
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed a reset package with the European Union at a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November 2026. The government says the deals could add up to 0.5% to UK GDP by 2040.
The package includes a Youth Experience Scheme, under which each side would let up to 100,000 young people live in the other's territory for up to three years. The two sides aim to apply it by 2028 and to have opportunities open by January 2030 at the latest. They also welcomed the conclusion of talks on linking their emissions trading schemes, aiming to apply that from 2028, which would mean mutual recognition of allowances and exemption from each other's carbon border taxes. The joint statement describes the food and agriculture (SPS) agreement as still to be concluded.
Tuition fees were not settled, and the two sides committed to try to reach a separate deal within six months. The government says nothing in the package requires UK taxpayers to pay into the EU budget. Nigel Farage accused Mr Burnham of betraying Brexit voters by moving back towards the single market.
levels.why: Why it matters: it is the biggest change to the UK's relationship with the EU in years and a major political dividing line.

levels.headline: UK and EU strike a reset deal, but key parts are still unfinished
levels.body:
Andy Burnham agreed a package of measures with the EU at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. The UK government says the deals could add up to 0.5% to the size of the economy by 2040.
A Youth Experience Scheme would let up to 100,000 young people from each side live in the other's territory for up to three years. It is meant to start by 2028, with places available by January 2030 at the latest. The two sides also finished talks on linking their carbon markets, which would let each recognise the other's permits and avoid carbon border charges, from 2028. The deal on food and farming rules, known as SPS, is described in the joint statement as still to be concluded.
Tuition fees remain unresolved, with six months set aside to try to agree them. The government says UK taxpayers will not have to pay into the EU budget under these deals. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage says the agreement betrays Brexit voters.
levels.why: It reshapes UK-EU trade and travel and is a flashpoint in domestic politics.

levels.headline: Burnham agrees a reset with the EU, while Farage says Brexit has been betrayed
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has agreed a package with the European Union at a summit in Brussels. The government estimates it could add up to 0.5% to UK economic output by 2040.
The package has three main parts. A youth scheme would allow up to 100,000 young people each way to live in the other side's territory for up to three years, with a target of 2028. A link between the UK and EU carbon markets would mean firms avoid extra carbon border charges. A deal to ease checks on food and farm goods is still being finished. Talks on cheaper university fees for EU students will carry on for up to six months.
Ministers say UK taxpayers will not pay into the EU budget because of these deals. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Mr Burnham was betraying people who voted for Brexit, though he admitted Brexit has failed on immigration.
levels.why: It could make trade and travel with the EU easier, but it is politically contested.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree a reset deal covering young people, carbon and food
levels.body:
The UK and the European Union have agreed a package of new deals at a summit in Brussels. The government says it could make the UK economy up to 0.5% bigger by 2040.
One deal is a youth scheme. Up to 100,000 young people from each side could live in the other's country for up to three years. It should start by 2028. Another deal links the two sides' systems for charging firms for carbon pollution, so businesses avoid extra border charges. A third deal, on food and farming checks, is not yet finished. Talks on tuition fees will continue for six months.
The government says UK taxpayers will not have to pay into the EU budget. Opponents, led by Nigel Farage, say the prime minister is undoing Brexit. Supporters say it cuts costs and red tape for firms and gives young people more chances.
levels.why: It changes how easily people and goods can move between the UK and the EU.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU agree new deals to make trade and travel easier
levels.body:
Britain's prime minister, Andy Burnham, has agreed new deals with the European Union. They were agreed at a meeting in Brussels on 20 November. The government says they could add up to 0.5% to the size of the UK economy by 2040. That means more money being made across the country over time.
The deals include a scheme for young people aged 18 to 31. Up to 100,000 from each side could live in the other's country for up to three years. Another deal would link the carbon markets, the systems that make companies pay for pollution, so firms do not face extra charges. A deal on food checks at borders is still being finished.
The government says taxpayers will not have to pay into the EU budget. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, says the deal betrays people who voted for Brexit.
levels.why: It affects prices, jobs and travel chances for ordinary people.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU agree new deals, though some are not finished
levels.body:
Britain left the European Union in 2020, and trading with it has been harder since. Now Prime Minister Andy Burnham has agreed new deals with the EU at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. The government says they could make the economy up to 0.5% bigger by 2040.
There is a scheme for young people, where up to 100,000 from each side could live in the other's country for up to three years. There is also a deal to link carbon markets, which are systems that make firms pay for pollution. A deal on food and farm checks is still being worked out, and so are university fees.
The government says UK taxpayers will not have to pay into the EU budget. Nigel Farage says the deal betrays people who voted for Brexit. Supporters say it cuts costs and paperwork.
levels.why: It could change prices, travel and job chances for young people.

levels.headline: The UK and the EU have agreed to work more closely together
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union in 2020. This is called Brexit. Since then, trade with the EU has had more checks and more paperwork. Now the UK's prime minister, Andy Burnham, has agreed new deals with the EU to ease some of that.
One deal lets young people live in the other side's country for up to three years. Up to 100,000 people from each side could take part. Another deal links two systems that make companies pay for causing pollution. A third deal, about checking food and farm goods, is not finished yet. The government says these deals could make the economy up to 0.5% bigger by 2040.
The government says UK taxpayers will not have to pay into the EU budget. Nigel Farage, who wanted Brexit, says this is a betrayal. Others say it will lower costs and help young people.
levels.why: It may make some goods cheaper and give young people new chances.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe are making new friendly deals
levels.body:
Britain used to be part of a group of countries called the European Union, or EU. It left in 2020. Since then, it has been harder and more costly to send goods between Britain and the EU. This week, the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, met EU leaders in Brussels. They agreed some new deals.
One deal is for young people. Up to 100,000 from each side could live in the other's country for up to three years. Another deal is about pollution. Companies pay for the pollution they make, and the two sides will now count each other's payments. A deal on food checks is not finished yet.
The government says this could help the economy grow by up to 0.5% by 2040. Some people, such as Nigel Farage, are angry. They say it goes against what voters chose when they backed Brexit.
levels.why: It could mean cheaper goods and more chances to live abroad.

levels.headline: Britain and its European neighbours agree to work together more
levels.body:
Britain is a country. The European Union, or EU, is a club of countries nearby. Britain left that club in 2020. Since then, sending things to and from the EU has been slower and costs more money.
This week, Britain's leader, Andy Burnham, went to a big meeting in Brussels. He agreed some new deals with the EU. One deal lets young people live in the other place for up to three years. Up to 100,000 people from each side can do this. Another deal is about pollution. Companies have to pay when they pollute. The two sides will now accept each other's payments. A deal about food checks is not done yet.
The government says these deals will help the country make more money. Some people are unhappy. They think Britain should stay away from the EU.
levels.why: It could help families by making some things cheaper.

levels.headline: Britain and its neighbours try to be better friends
levels.body:
Imagine your school and the school next door had a falling out. For a while, you could not share things or visit each other easily. Now the two schools have agreed to be friendlier.
That is a bit like what has happened between Britain and the European Union, a group of countries close by. Britain left the group in 2020. This week, Britain's leader, Andy Burnham, met them and agreed some new deals. Young people could go and live in the other place for a few years. Companies will find it easier to trade. Some food checks may also get easier later on.
The government says this could help the country earn more money in future. Some grown-ups are cross about it. They think Britain should keep more distance. Others think being friends is better for everyone.
levels.why: It might make life a little easier and cheaper for lots of families.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 3.7% at 6,910.39 as Wall Street's correction deepens; Nasdaq falls 5.3%

terms.meaning: A fall of 10% or more from a recent high in a market index.
A stock index dominated by technology companies.
The return investors get for lending to the US government; it moves opposite to bond prices.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 3.7% at 6,910.39 as Wall Street's correction deepens; Nasdaq falls 5.3%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Friday 20 November 2026, falling 3.70% to 6,910.39, which left it about 10% below its record closing high. That is a correction. The session was complete when these figures were reported.
CNBC reported that the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73, leaving it down 2.7% for 2026. Trading Economics gave a slightly different Dow close of about 48,034, so figures vary a little by source. For the week, CNBC said the Dow fell around 8%, its worst week since March 2020, and the S&P 500 fell about 8.6%, its worst since April 2025.
CNBC pointed to the Anthropic IPO, troubles at Nvidia, and worries about the Federal Reserve and inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5% earlier in the week before safe-haven buying pulled it back below that level on Friday.
levels.why: Why it matters: falling share prices hit pensions, savings and business confidence well beyond the US.

levels.headline: Wall Street sinks again on Friday: S&P 500 down 3.7% and in a correction
levels.body:
US stocks fell sharply on Friday 20 November 2026. The S&P 500 closed down 3.70% at 6,910.39, about 10% below its record high, which counts as a correction. The trading day had finished.
CNBC reported that the Dow fell 1.93% to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% to 22,617.73, which means it is down 2.7% so far this year. Another data provider put the Dow slightly lower, so exact figures differ by source. Over the week the Dow lost around 8%, its worst week since March 2020, and the S&P 500 lost roughly 8.6%.
CNBC linked the sell-off to concern about artificial intelligence shares, including problems at Nvidia and the Anthropic stock market debut, and to fears over inflation and higher US interest rates. Government bond yields, which had topped 5%, fell back as investors looked for safer places to put money.
levels.why: Big share falls can weaken savings and make firms more cautious about spending.

levels.headline: US shares fall hard, with the S&P 500 down 3.7% on Friday
levels.body:
US shares had a very bad Friday. The S&P 500, a measure of 500 big American companies, closed down 3.70% at 6,910.39. That is about 10% below its all-time high, which investors call a correction. The session was over when these numbers were reported.
The Dow Jones, which tracks 30 large firms, fell 1.93% to 48,147.33 according to CNBC. The Nasdaq, which has many tech companies, fell 5.28% to 22,617.73 and is now lower than where it began the year. Different sources give slightly different Dow figures. Over the whole week, the Dow lost around 8% and the S&P 500 about 8.6%.
CNBC said the causes included worry about artificial intelligence companies such as Nvidia, the Anthropic share launch, and fears that high inflation will lead the US central bank to raise interest rates again.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and how confident businesses feel.

levels.headline: US shares fall sharply, with the S&P 500 down 3.7%
levels.body:
Shares in the United States fell sharply on Friday. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big American companies, closed down 3.70% at 6,910.39. It is about 10% below its highest level, which is called a correction. The trading day was over when these figures were reported.
The Dow Jones fell 1.93% to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, fell 5.28% to 22,617.73. Over the week, the Dow lost about 8%. CNBC said investors were worried about artificial intelligence companies, trouble at chipmaker Nvidia and the chance of more interest rate rises. Interest rates are the cost of borrowing, and higher ones can make shares look less attractive to investors.
levels.why: It can hit savings and pensions linked to shares.

levels.headline: Wall Street has a big sell-off, with tech shares hit hardest
levels.body:
Shares in the United States fell sharply on Friday. The S&P 500, which follows 500 of the country's biggest companies, closed down 3.70% at 6,910.39. It is now about 10% below its highest level. When a market falls that far, it is called a correction.
The Dow Jones, a group of 30 big firms, fell 1.93% to 48,147.33, says CNBC. The Nasdaq, which is full of technology companies, dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73. It has now lost ground since the start of the year. Over the week, the Dow lost about 8% and the S&P 500 about 8.6%.
CNBC said investors were worried about artificial intelligence companies, problems at chipmaker Nvidia, and the chance of higher US interest rates. Interest rates are the price of borrowing money, and higher ones can make shares less attractive.
levels.why: It can reduce the value of savings and pensions linked to shares.

levels.headline: US stock markets fall sharply on Friday
levels.body:
The stock market is a place where people buy and sell small pieces of companies, called shares. On Friday, US share prices fell a lot. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big American companies, closed down 3.7%. It ended at 6,910.39. That is about 10% below its highest ever level, so it is now in what experts call a correction.
The Dow Jones fell 1.93% to 48,147.33. The Nasdaq, which is full of tech firms, fell 5.28% to 22,617.73. Across the week, the Dow lost about 8%, and the S&P 500 lost about 8.6%.
Reporters said people are worried about artificial intelligence companies and about prices rising too fast. That could lead to higher interest rates, which make borrowing money cost more.
levels.why: Pensions and savings are often linked to share prices.

levels.headline: Share prices in America fell a lot on Friday
levels.body:
A share is a small piece of a company. People buy shares hoping they will be worth more later. On Friday, many share prices in the United States went down. A well-known measure called the S&P 500 fell by 3.7%. It finished the day at 6,910.39. That is about one tenth lower than its best ever level. People call that a correction.
Two other measures also fell. The Dow Jones went down 1.93% to 48,147.33. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology firms, went down 5.28% to 22,617.73. Over the whole week, the Dow fell about 8%.
Reporters said people are worried about companies using artificial intelligence, and about prices going up too fast. Prices going up is called inflation. It might make borrowing money cost more.
levels.why: Money saved for pensions is often placed in shares.

levels.headline: Share prices in America dropped a lot on Friday
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. People buy shares hoping they will be worth more later. On Friday, lots of share prices in the United States dropped. A big measure called the S&P 500 fell by 3.7% and finished at 6,910.39. That is about a tenth lower than its best ever level.
The Dow Jones fell 1.93% and the Nasdaq, which has lots of technology companies, fell 5.28%. Over the whole week the Dow lost about 8%.
People are worried about companies that make computer brains, called artificial intelligence. They are also worried that prices are going up too fast. If that goes on, borrowing money could cost more, so some people sold their shares.
levels.why: Many grown-ups save for retirement using shares.

levels.headline: American share prices tumble
levels.body:
Shares are tiny parts of companies. People buy them and hope they grow in value. On Friday, share prices in America fell a lot. A big measure called the S&P 500 went down 3.7%. It ended the day at 6,910.39. That is about 10% lower than its top level. This is called a correction.
Two more measures went down as well. The Dow Jones fell 1.93%. The Nasdaq fell 5.28%. The Nasdaq has many technology firms in it. Over the week, the Dow lost about 8%.
People are worried about companies that use artificial intelligence, or AI. They are also worried that prices are going up too fast. If that goes on, borrowing money may cost more. That makes some investors want to sell their shares.
levels.why: Many grown-ups save for retirement using shares.

levels.headline: Prices of company shares drop in America
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet shop where children swap stickers. One day, lots of children decide their stickers are not worth as much, and they all want to sell at once. The price of stickers drops fast.
Something like that happened in America on Friday, but with shares, which are small parts of real companies. A big measure called the S&P 500 fell by 3.7%. It is now about 10% lower than its best ever level. Other measures, the Dow and the Nasdaq, fell too. The Nasdaq fell by more than 5%.
Grown-ups say they are worried about computer companies and about prices going up too much. Because of that, many people sold their shares. When lots of people sell at once, prices fall.
levels.why: Grown-ups save money in shares, so big falls can worry them.

headline: UK inflation at 3.6% and Bank Rate at 4%: markets expect a second Bank of England rise on 17 December

terms.meaning: How quickly prices are rising across the economy.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences loan and savings rates.
The nine-member group at the Bank that sets interest rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation at 3.6% and Bank Rate at 4%: markets expect a second Bank of England rise on 17 December
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October 2026, a one-year high, with energy costs, including record diesel prices, the main driver. The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November, its first rise in over three years, and has warned inflation could approach 5% by mid-2027.
Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point increase and one wanted a half-point rise. Governor Andrew Bailey said the November move should not be seen as the first of an inevitable long series, but that unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved it does not seem likely to be the last.
Money markets put the chance of a quarter-point rise at the next decision, on 17 December, at roughly 80% to 90%, according to CNBC citing LSEG data. Recent wage data gave policymakers more confidence that the economy can withstand another increase.
levels.why: Why it matters: higher rates raise the cost of mortgages and loans, while rising prices squeeze household budgets.

levels.headline: Prices rising at 3.6% and another Bank of England rate rise looks likely
levels.body:
UK inflation climbed to 3.6% in the year to October, the highest in a year, mainly because of energy costs and record diesel prices. On 5 November the Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4%, the first rise in more than three years. The Bank has warned that inflation could get close to 5% by the middle of 2027.
Eight of the nine members of the rate-setting committee backed a quarter-point rise, while one wanted a half-point rise. Governor Andrew Bailey said it should not be seen as the start of a long run of increases, but added that without an end to the Middle East conflict it is unlikely to be the last.
Markets now think there is about an 80% to 90% chance of another quarter-point rise on 17 December. Wage figures have made policymakers more confident that the economy can cope with it.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make borrowing dearer even as prices squeeze budgets.

levels.headline: UK prices rise 3.6% a year and interest rates may go up again in December
levels.body:
Inflation, the rate at which prices rise, hit 3.6% in the year to October. That is the highest for a year. The main cause is energy, with record diesel prices pushing up the cost of getting goods around. The Bank of England has warned inflation could come close to 5% by the middle of next year.
To slow price rises, the Bank raised its main interest rate to 4% on 5 November. It was the first rise in over three years. Eight members of the committee voted for it and one wanted a bigger rise. Governor Andrew Bailey said more rises are possible if the Middle East conflict is not resolved.
Investors now expect a further quarter-point rise on 17 December, with chances put at around 80% to 90%. Stronger wage data has made the Bank more comfortable with that.
levels.why: Mortgages and loans could cost more while shop and fuel prices stay high.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster and interest rates could go up again
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up over time. In the year to October it was 3.6%, the highest in a year. Fuel is a big reason. Diesel prices hit a record, which makes it dearer to move goods around the country. The Bank of England says inflation could get close to 5% by the middle of next year.
The Bank tries to slow prices by raising interest rates, the cost of borrowing money. On 5 November it raised its main rate to 4%, the first rise in over three years. Governor Andrew Bailey said that more rises could follow if the Middle East conflict carries on.
Investors think the Bank will raise rates by a quarter of a percentage point again on 17 December. They put the chance at about 80% to 90%. Good pay figures made that more likely.
levels.why: It affects the cost of mortgages, loans and weekly shopping.

levels.headline: UK prices keep rising, so interest rates may go up again
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices rise. In October, prices were 3.6% higher than a year before. That is the highest in a year. Fuel is a big reason. Diesel has been very costly, and that makes goods dearer to deliver. The Bank of England, which looks after the country's money, thinks inflation could get close to 5% by next summer.
The Bank has a tool to fight rising prices. It raises the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing. On 5 November it raised the rate to 4%. That was the first rise for more than three years. Its governor, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could come if the war in the Middle East goes on.
Many investors now expect a small rise on 17 December. They think it is around 80% to 90% likely.
levels.why: Home loans and shop prices could both cost families more.

levels.headline: Prices are rising and the Bank of England may raise rates again
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up. In the UK, prices in October were 3.6% higher than a year before. Fuel is a big reason, because diesel has been very costly. The Bank of England, which looks after the country's money, thinks inflation could get close to 5% next summer.
To slow prices, the Bank raises its interest rate, which is the price of borrowing. On 5 November it raised the rate to 4%. Its governor, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could follow if the war in the Middle East goes on.
Many experts now think the Bank will raise the rate again on 17 December. That could make mortgages and loans cost more, even while shop prices stay high for families.
levels.why: Families may pay more for loans while prices stay high.

levels.headline: Prices are going up and loans may cost more
levels.body:
Prices in the UK have been going up. This is called inflation. In October, things cost 3.6% more than a year earlier. For example, something that cost £100 now costs £103.60. Fuel is a big reason, because diesel has been very expensive.
The Bank of England wants to slow price rises. It does this by making borrowing more expensive, with a higher interest rate. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. On 5 November the Bank raised its rate to 4%. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said it could go up again if the war in the Middle East carries on.
Many people who work with money think the Bank will raise the rate again on 17 December. They think it is very likely, about 80% to 90%.
levels.why: Families with loans or mortgages may have to pay more each month.

levels.headline: Shop prices are rising and the Bank may raise interest rates
levels.body:
Inflation means that prices go up. If a sweet cost £1 last year and costs £1.04 now, that is inflation. In the UK in October, prices were 3.6% higher than a year before. Fuel was a big reason. Diesel was very expensive, so it cost more to move goods around.
The Bank of England is a special bank that looks after the country's money. It wants prices to stop rising so fast. So it raised the interest rate to 4% on 5 November. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. A higher rate makes people borrow less and spend less. Its boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises may come.
Many experts think the Bank will raise the rate again on 17 December.
levels.why: It can make things cost more for people who borrow money.

levels.headline: Prices are going up, and borrowing money may get dearer
levels.body:
Do you remember when a chocolate bar was cheaper? Prices going up is called inflation. In the UK, prices are now 3.6% higher than a year ago. A big reason is that fuel costs a lot. Fuel is used to carry food and toys to the shops, so they cost more.
There is a very important bank called the Bank of England. It tries to stop prices from rising too fast. It can do this by changing the interest rate. Interest is a bit of extra money you pay when you borrow. The bank raised the rate on 5 November. The boss, Andrew Bailey, said it might go up again.
Many grown-ups who watch money think the rate will go up again on 17 December. That would make borrowing cost more.
levels.why: Grown-ups may have less money left over for treats.

levels.headline: Why things cost more and what the big bank is doing
levels.body:
Imagine you get pocket money every week, but the sweets at the shop keep getting dearer. Your money buys less than before. That is what grown-ups call inflation. In the UK, prices are now 3.6% higher than last year. Fuel costing so much is a big reason.
There is a very big bank for the whole country called the Bank of England. It tries to keep prices steady. One thing it can do is make borrowing money cost a bit more, because then people spend less, and prices stop rising so fast. It did this on 5 November. It might do it again on 17 December.
That is good for slowing prices. But it can be tricky for families who have borrowed money, because they pay back a little more.
levels.why: Families may need to be careful with money for a while.

headline: UK retail sales volumes rise 0.7% in October, with online sales values up 1.5%

terms.meaning: The amount of goods sold, with the effect of price changes removed.
Statistics tweaked to remove regular seasonal patterns so months can be compared fairly.
Shops that sell items other than food, such as clothes and household goods.

levels.headline: UK retail sales volumes rise 0.7% in October, with online sales values up 1.5%
levels.body:
Retail sales volumes in Great Britain rose 0.7% in October 2026, following a 0.6% fall in September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in its first estimate, released on 20 November. Volumes were 2.3% higher than in October 2025, and rose 0.4% in the three months to October compared with the three months to July.
Food stores rose as supermarkets reported an uplift in purchases of emergency items such as UHT milk and tinned goods. Non-food store volumes rose 1.1% on the month. Automotive fuel volumes fell back to August levels as prices rose for a third consecutive month.
Online sales values rose 1.5% after a 0.3% fall in September, and were 9.7% higher than a year earlier. Separately, the CBI's retail sales balance improved to minus 10 in November from minus 55 in October, though the CBI warned the outlook remains fragile because households are cautious and fuel costs are higher.
levels.why: Why it matters: shop spending is a key sign of how confident households feel as prices rise.

levels.headline: Shoppers spend more in October, with sales volumes up 0.7%
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics said that the amount bought in British shops rose 0.7% in October 2026, after falling 0.6% in September. This first estimate came out on 20 November. Volumes were 2.3% higher than a year earlier and up 0.4% over the latest three months.
Supermarkets reported extra buying of emergency items such as UHT milk and tinned goods. Non-food stores saw volumes rise 1.1%. Fuel sales volumes fell back to August levels because petrol and diesel prices rose for a third month running.
Online spending was up 1.5% in value and 9.7% higher than a year ago. A separate CBI survey showed retailers feeling less gloomy in November, with its balance improving to minus 10 from minus 55. The CBI said the outlook is still fragile, because households are cautious and fuel is costly.
levels.why: It shows whether people are still spending as living costs rise.

levels.headline: UK shops had a better October, with sales up 0.7%
levels.body:
The amount people bought in British shops went up 0.7% in October 2026. The Office for National Statistics, which collects official figures, reported this on 20 November. In September, sales had fallen 0.6%. Compared with October last year, sales were 2.3% higher.
Some of the rise came from food shops. Supermarkets said people bought more emergency items such as long-life milk and tinned food. Shops selling other goods, such as clothes, saw a 1.1% rise. Buying fuel fell because prices went up for a third month in a row.
Online shopping grew too, by 1.5%, and is 9.7% higher than a year ago. A survey by the CBI, a business group, found shops are less gloomy than in October, but warned that shoppers are still careful and fuel costs are high.
levels.why: People's spending is a sign of how the economy is doing.

levels.headline: UK shoppers spent more in October, with sales up 0.7%
levels.body:
The amount bought in British shops rose 0.7% in October, according to the Office for National Statistics, the body that produces official figures. It had fallen 0.6% in September. Compared with a year before, sales were 2.3% higher.
Supermarkets sold more emergency items like long-life milk and tinned food. Shops selling other goods saw sales rise 1.1%. Fuel sales fell because petrol and diesel prices rose for a third month in a row. Online spending rose 1.5%, and is almost 10% above last year.
A business group called the CBI said shops feel less gloomy now. But it warned that households are still cautious with money and that fuel costs are high, so the outlook is not secure.
levels.why: It shows whether families feel able to spend as prices rise.

levels.headline: British shoppers spent more in October
levels.body:
People in Britain bought more in shops in October. The Office for National Statistics, the body that produces official figures, said the amount sold rose by 0.7% compared with September. In September it had fallen by 0.6%. Compared with a year earlier, shops sold 2.3% more.
Supermarkets sold more emergency items such as long-life milk and tinned food. Other shops, such as clothes shops, sold 1.1% more. Shops selling fuel for cars sold less, because petrol and diesel got dearer for the third month in a row.
Buying online went up by 1.5%, and it is almost 10% higher than a year ago. A business group called the CBI said shops are feeling a bit better now. But it warned that shoppers are still being careful with money and fuel costs a lot.
levels.why: Shop sales show how comfortable families feel with their money.

levels.headline: Shops sold more in October
levels.body:
Every month, the Office for National Statistics counts how much people buy in shops. This is what they found for October. People bought 0.7% more than in September. In September, they had bought 0.6% less. Compared with a year ago, shops sold 2.3% more.
Supermarkets sold more long-life milk and tinned food. Other shops, such as clothes shops, sold 1.1% more. Petrol and diesel sales went down, because the price of fuel kept going up for the third month in a row.
More people shopped online too. Online sales went up by 1.5%. A group of business experts called the CBI says shops are feeling better. But it also warns that people are still careful with their money, and fuel costs a lot.
levels.why: It tells us if families feel able to spend.

levels.headline: People bought a bit more from shops in October
levels.body:
Each month, a team of experts counts how much people buy in shops across Britain. In October, people bought a bit more than in September. It was 0.7% more. Think of 1,000 shopping trips in September. In October, that would be about 1,007. In September, people had bought a little less than in August.
Supermarkets sold more tins of food and long-life milk. Other shops, like clothes shops, sold a bit more too. Shops that sell petrol and diesel sold less, because those got dearer.
More people shopped on the internet as well. A group of business people called the CBI says shop owners feel happier than last month. But shoppers are still careful with their money.
levels.why: When people spend more, shops and the wider economy do better.

levels.headline: Shops sold a bit more in October

Each month, experts count how much people buy in shops in Britain. In October, people bought a bit more than in September. It was a rise of 0.7%. In September, people had bought a little less than the month before.

levels.headline: Shops did a bit better last month

Every month, grown-ups count how much people buy in shops. Last month, October, people bought a little more than the month before. That is good news for shops. It was a small rise of 0.7%. The month before, people had bought a bit less.
Some people bought extra tins of food and cartons of long-life milk. Clothes shops and other shops did a bit better too. But petrol stations sold less, because petrol and diesel cost more now.

levels.headline: People are spending a little more in the shops
levels.body:
Think about your local shop. If lots of people come in and buy things, the shop does well. If fewer come in, the shop does badly. Last month, October, a few more people bought things in British shops than the month before. The rise was small, but it is good news for shop owners.
Some people bought extra tins of food. Others bought clothes and other things. Fewer people bought petrol, because it costs more now. Many people also bought things on the internet instead of going out.
Shop experts say owners are feeling a bit happier. But they say families are still careful with their money. When prices are high, people think hard before they spend.
levels.why: When families spend, shops can keep their staff and stay open.

headline: Macron warns of 'new level' of Russian aggression as Estonia closes border and missiles land in Poland

terms.meaning: A military alliance of North American and European countries that promise to defend each other.
Deliberate damage or disruption, often secret.
Russia's military intelligence agency.

levels.headline: Macron warns of 'new level' of Russian aggression as Estonia closes border and missiles land in Poland
levels.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron warned on 21 November 2026 that a run of incidents across Europe signals a "new level of aggression" by Russia. He wrote that several European partners and allies had again faced serious incidents.
Polish authorities said two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland while allied nations were holding military exercises there. Estonia said it will close its road border crossings with Russia from 1 December, linking the decision to a sabotage attempt against drone maker Threod Systems that it says the GRU ordered. Rail services are unaffected and the measure could be reviewed in six months. Denmark's intelligence service accused Russian intelligence of an assassination attempt against a Ukrainian American citizen near Copenhagen in September, according to Euronews.
The remarks followed large Russian strikes across Ukraine that killed at least seven people in Kyiv and damaged bridges over the Dnipro River. Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles.
levels.why: Why it matters: incidents on NATO territory raise the risk of a wider conflict in Europe.

levels.headline: Macron says Russia has reached a 'new level of aggression' after incidents in Poland and Estonia
levels.body:
President Emmanuel Macron of France said on 21 November that several European countries had faced serious incidents which show a new level of Russian aggression.
Polish authorities said two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone came down inside Poland during allied military exercises. Estonia announced it will shut its road border crossings with Russia from 1 December after what it says was a sabotage attempt against the drone maker Threod Systems, ordered by Russian military intelligence. Trains will still run, and the closure may be reviewed in six months. Denmark's security service also accused Russian agents of an assassination attempt near Copenhagen in September.
The warnings came after Russia hit Ukraine with a huge barrage. President Zelenskyy said it included over 400 drones and more than 110 missiles. At least seven people died in Kyiv and key bridges were damaged.
levels.why: It shows how far the war in Ukraine is spilling into the rest of Europe.

levels.headline: France's president warns Russia is becoming more aggressive towards Europe
levels.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that Russia has reached a new level of aggression. He said on 21 November that several European countries had faced serious incidents in recent days.
Poland said two Russian missiles and a drone crashed on its land while allied armies were training there. Estonia will close its road crossings with Russia from 1 December. It blames a Russian military intelligence plot to sabotage a drone company. Trains will keep running. Denmark has also accused Russian agents of an attempted killing near Copenhagen in September.
The warnings came after a huge Russian attack on Ukraine. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russia used more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles. At least seven people were killed in Kyiv, and bridges were damaged.
levels.why: It raises worries about the safety of countries that border Russia.

levels.headline: Europe faces more Russian incidents, says Macron
levels.body:
The president of France, Emmanuel Macron, says Russia is behaving more aggressively. He spoke on 21 November after several scary events in Europe.
Poland said two Russian missiles and a drone fell on its land. This happened while other countries' armies were training there. Estonia, a small country next to Russia, will close its road crossings with Russia from 1 December. It says Russia's military spies tried to damage a drone company. Trains will still run. Denmark says Russian agents tried to kill someone near its capital in September.
These events came after a huge Russian attack on Ukraine. Ukraine's president said Russia fired over 400 drones and over 110 missiles. At least seven people died in the city of Kyiv, and some bridges were hit.
levels.why: Many European countries now worry about their own safety.

levels.headline: France's leader says Russia is getting more dangerous for Europe
levels.body:
France's leader, Emmanuel Macron, says Russia is acting in a more dangerous way. He said this on 21 November. He talked about several bad events in Europe in the past few days.
Poland said two Russian missiles and a drone landed on its ground. Soldiers from other countries were training there at the time. Estonia is a small country next to Russia. It said it will close its road border with Russia from 1 December. It says Russian spies tried to damage a drone company. Trains will still cross. Denmark says Russian agents tried to harm someone near its capital city.
These events came after a very big attack on Ukraine. Ukraine's president said Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles. At least seven people died.
levels.why: It makes people in nearby countries worry about being safe.

levels.headline: France's president says Russia is becoming more dangerous to Europe
levels.body:
The president of France, Emmanuel Macron, says Russia is acting more aggressively. He said on 21 November that several European countries had faced serious incidents lately.
Poland said two Russian missiles and a drone crashed on its land while other countries' armies were training there. Estonia, a small country next to Russia, will close its road border crossings with Russia from 1 December. It says Russian military intelligence tried to sabotage a drone company. Trains will keep running. Denmark says Russian agents tried to harm someone near its capital in September.
This came after a huge Russian attack on Ukraine, with more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, according to Ukraine's president. At least seven people died in Kyiv.
levels.why: It makes countries near Russia worry about their own safety.

levels.headline: Russia is causing trouble in Europe, says French leader
levels.body:
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, says Russia is causing more trouble than before. Russia is a big country in the east of Europe. It has been fighting a war in Ukraine for years.
Macron said that in the last few days, several European countries had scary problems. In Poland, two Russian rockets and a drone fell on the ground. Estonia is a small country next to Russia. It will close its road border with Russia from 1 December, because it says Russian spies tried to break things. Denmark says Russian agents tried to hurt someone.
The war in Ukraine is still going on. Russia sent more than 400 drones and over 110 rockets in one attack. At least seven people died in Kyiv.
levels.why: Countries near Russia worry the war might spread.

levels.headline: A leader says Russia is being more dangerous
levels.body:
Russia is a big country. It has been fighting a war with its neighbour, Ukraine. The president of France, Emmanuel Macron, says Russia has become more dangerous. He said that other countries in Europe have had scary problems too.
In Poland, two Russian rockets and a flying machine called a drone fell down. In Estonia, a small country next to Russia, leaders will close the road border from 1 December. They say Russian spies tried to wreck a drone factory. Denmark says Russian agents tried to hurt a person.
The war in Ukraine is still going on too. In one night, Russia sent more than 400 drones and over 110 rockets. At least seven people died.
levels.why: People in nearby countries are worried about their safety.

levels.headline: Some countries feel unsafe because of a war nearby
levels.body:
Imagine two neighbours fighting over a fence. Some other neighbours worry the fight might spill over into their gardens. That is a little like what is happening in Europe now.
Russia has been fighting a war with Ukraine. This week, the leader of France, Emmanuel Macron, said Russia is being more dangerous. Some rockets and a drone from Russia landed in Poland. A small country called Estonia will close its road border with Russia. Its leaders say spies from Russia tried to break things there.
These countries are working together to stay safe. They want the fighting to stay far from their homes. But many grown-ups feel worried.
levels.why: It matters because many families in Europe are worried about safety.

levels.headline: There is a big fight far away, and nearby places are worried
levels.body:
Imagine a big argument in the playground between two groups of children. Some other children stand nearby and feel nervous that it might spread to them.
That is a bit like what is happening in Europe. Russia is fighting a war against Ukraine. A leader in France, called Emmanuel Macron, says Russia is behaving worse than before. Some rockets landed in a country called Poland. Another country, Estonia, is closing a road to Russia because it thinks spies from Russia tried to cause damage.
The countries that are not fighting do not want to be pulled in. They are talking to each other and trying to stay safe. Grown-ups hope the fighting stops.
levels.why: Grown-ups want everyone, including children, to stay safe.

headline: Iran reports new attacks on US bases in Bahrain as tanker convoy readies to test US blockade

terms.meaning: Using warships to stop ships from entering or leaving a place.
A narrow sea route between the Gulf and the open ocean through which a large share of the world's oil passes.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful armed force.

levels.headline: Iran reports new attacks on US bases in Bahrain as tanker convoy readies to test US blockade
levels.body:
Euronews reported on 21 November 2026 that Iran launched two waves of drone and ballistic missile attacks on four US bases in Bahrain on Saturday night. Bahrain warned residents to shelter. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed hits on Patriot batteries and a radar, but Bahrain and the US military did not confirm the claims.
More than 14 Iranian tankers are reportedly lined up at Kharg Island, poised to try to break the US naval blockade of Iran's oil exports. Iran's deputy foreign minister called the blockade "an act of war" and warned of a "fierce military response" if the convoy is engaged. The US military says it is "strictly enforcing" the blockade and has struck Iranian missile launchers in the south of the country.
Mediation by Qatar and Pakistan continues. Iran's foreign minister said reopening the Strait of Hormuz would be "not difficult" if the US accepted Iran's conditions, above all an end to the blockade. Many details come from Iranian statements and are not independently confirmed.
levels.why: Why it matters: the Strait of Hormuz carries a large share of the world's oil, so conflict there can raise fuel prices everywhere.

levels.headline: Iran says it hit US bases in Bahrain as a tanker convoy prepares to challenge the blockade
levels.body:
Iran reportedly launched two waves of drone and missile attacks on four US bases in Bahrain on Saturday night, according to Euronews. Bahrain told people to shelter. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit two Patriot missile batteries and a radar, but Bahrain and the US did not confirm this.
More than 14 tankers are said to be gathered at Kharg Island, ready to try to run the US naval blockade of Iranian oil. Iran called the blockade "an act of war" and threatened a "fierce military response" if the convoy is stopped. The US says it is enforcing the blockade strictly and has attacked Iranian missile launchers in southern Iran.
Qatar and Pakistan are mediating. Iran's foreign minister said reopening the Strait of Hormuz would not be difficult if the US ended the blockade. Most claims come from Iranian statements and are unconfirmed.
levels.why: A clash at sea could disrupt oil supplies and push up fuel prices.

levels.headline: Iran and the US edge closer to confrontation over oil shipping
levels.body:
Iran says it attacked US military bases in Bahrain on Saturday night, using drones and missiles. Bahrain told its people to take shelter. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed it hit missile defences and a radar, but Bahrain and the US did not confirm that.
More than 14 Iranian oil tankers are reportedly waiting at Kharg Island. They may try to get past a US naval blockade, which stops Iran selling its oil by sea. Iran called the blockade an act of war and warned of a strong response. The US says it is enforcing the blockade and has struck Iranian missile launchers.
Qatar and Pakistan are trying to broker talks. Iran says reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil route, would be easy if the blockade ended. Most details are Iranian claims.
levels.why: It could affect the price of oil and petrol around the world.

levels.headline: Iran and the US edge nearer to confrontation over oil ships
levels.body:
Iran says it attacked US military bases in Bahrain on Saturday night using drones and missiles. Bahrain told people to take shelter. Iran said it hit missile defences and a radar, but Bahrain and the US did not confirm this.
The US navy is blocking Iranian oil exports, which is called a blockade. More than 14 Iranian tankers are reportedly waiting at Kharg Island to try to get past. Iran calls the blockade an act of war and warns of a strong response. The US says it is enforcing it strictly.
Qatar and Pakistan are trying to mediate. The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route for much of the world's oil, is close by. Most details come from Iran and are not independently confirmed.
levels.why: It could affect oil supplies and fuel prices worldwide.

levels.headline: Iran and the US trade blows over a blocked oil route
levels.body:
Iran says it attacked US military bases in the country of Bahrain on Saturday night with drones and missiles. Bahrain told people to stay safe indoors. Iran said it hit some missile defences, but Bahrain and the US did not say that was true.
The US Navy is stopping Iranian oil ships from leaving. This is called a blockade. More than 14 Iranian oil tankers are waiting to try to get past it. Iran says the blockade is an act of war and has promised a strong response. The US says it will keep the blockade in place.
Qatar and Pakistan are trying to help the two sides talk. A lot of the world's oil travels through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. Most details come from Iran and cannot be checked.
levels.why: Fighting near key oil routes can make fuel more expensive for everyone.

levels.headline: Iran and the United States are in a standoff at sea
levels.body:
Iran says it attacked American military bases in a small country called Bahrain on Saturday night. It says it used drones and missiles. Bahrain told its people to take shelter. Bahrain and the US did not agree that Iran hit what it said it hit.
The American navy is stopping Iranian oil ships. That is called a blockade. More than 14 Iranian oil tankers are waiting to try to sail past. Iran says this blockade is like starting a war. It has promised to fight back if its ships are stopped.
Other countries, Qatar and Pakistan, are trying to help the two sides talk. A very busy sea route for oil, the Strait of Hormuz, is nearby. Most of this news comes from Iran and cannot be checked.
levels.why: The oil that passes there is used to make petrol for cars.

levels.headline: A dangerous standoff is happening near where lots of oil travels
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid that is made into petrol for cars. A lot of it travels on ships through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. Right now, there is a standoff near there.
Iran says it attacked American bases in a small country called Bahrain. It says it used drones and missiles. The American navy is stopping Iranian oil ships from leaving, which is called a blockade. Iran has about 14 oil ships ready to try to get past. Iran says it will fight back if they are stopped.
Other countries, Qatar and Pakistan, are trying to get both sides to talk. Most of the news comes from Iran and nobody has checked it. If the fight gets worse, petrol could become dearer.
levels.why: It matters because it could make fuel more expensive.

levels.headline: Two sides argue over a blocked sea route for oil
levels.body:
Iran and the United States are in a standoff at sea. The American navy is stopping Iranian oil ships from leaving. This is called a blockade. Iran says that is very unfair, like starting a war, and says it attacked American bases in a small country called Bahrain. Bahrain and the US have not said Iran hit what it claimed.
More than 14 Iranian oil ships are waiting to try to sail past the navy. Iran has promised a strong response if they are stopped.
Qatar and Pakistan are trying to help both sides talk. A lot of the world's oil goes through a narrow sea route nearby, the Strait of Hormuz. Most of this news comes from Iran and cannot be checked yet.
levels.why: It matters because oil makes petrol, so costs could rise for families.

levels.headline: Two sides are in a big argument about ships
levels.body:
Imagine two groups arguing about a road that everyone needs. One group stands in the road and will not let the other group's lorries pass. The other group gets angry and says it will fight back.
That is a bit like the standoff in the Middle East. The American navy is stopping oil ships from Iran from sailing out. Iran says that is very unfair. It says it has attacked some American bases. Nobody else has checked this. Iran has lots of oil ships ready to try to sail past.
Other countries are trying to help the two sides talk. The sea route is very important because lots of the world's oil goes that way. Grown-ups hope the argument ends peacefully.
levels.why: Oil makes petrol, so a fight over it can affect everyone's costs.

levels.headline: Two big groups are arguing, and ships are caught in the middle
levels.body:
Imagine a playground gate that everyone must go through. One group of children blocks the gate, so another group cannot get out. The blocked group gets very cross. It says it will push its way through.
Something like this is happening at sea in the Middle East. The American navy is blocking oil ships from Iran. Iran says this is unfair. It says it has attacked some American bases in answer. Nobody has checked if that is true. Iran has lots of ships ready to try to sail through.
Other countries are acting like teachers. They are trying to get both sides to talk. Grown-ups worry because a lot of the world's oil goes through that sea route.
levels.why: If the oil stops flowing, petrol for cars can cost more.

headline: Anthropic's record IPO collides with Wall Street's worst tech week since 2020 as shares end first week at $88.91

terms.meaning: Initial public offering: a company's first sale of shares to the public on a stock exchange.
The total value of all of a company's shares.
Extra shares that underwriters can sell on top of the planned number if demand is strong.

levels.headline: Anthropic's record IPO collides with Wall Street's worst tech week since 2020 as shares end first week at $88.91
levels.body:
Anthropic listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday 19 November 2026, in what CNBC called a record IPO. The shares were priced at $83, opened at $111.50 and closed their first day at $97.17, 17% above the IPO price, giving a market value of about $1.8 trillion.
The stock then fell about 8.5% on Friday to close at $88.91 as the AI sell-off continued. CNBC reported that, with the overallotment, Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in total. Other reports quote different figures for total proceeds, depending on whether a private placement is counted.
The debut came in a bad week for tech. Led by a 23% plunge in Nvidia, its sharpest weekly drop in 18 years, the Nasdaq fell about 10% in five trading days, its worst week since early 2020. The S&P 500 and Dow both entered correction territory.
levels.why: Why it matters: the biggest AI listing in history could not stop a market sell-off, raising questions about how much investors will pay for AI.

levels.headline: Anthropic shares fall in first week after record stock market debut
levels.body:
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday 19 November. The shares were priced at $83, opened at $111.50 and ended the first day at $97.17, which is 17% above the IPO price and values the company at around $1.8 trillion.
On Friday the shares dropped about 8.5% to $88.91 as worries about artificial intelligence stocks weighed on the market. CNBC said that with extra shares sold by the banks, Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in total, though other reports give different totals.
The launch came in a rough week for technology. Nvidia fell 23%, its worst week in 18 years, and the Nasdaq lost about 10%, its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020. The S&P 500 and Dow both fell into correction territory.
levels.why: It tests how much investors really want to pay for artificial intelligence firms.

levels.headline: Anthropic's big stock market launch is followed by a fall in its share price
levels.body:
Anthropic, the AI company, began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the code ANT. Its shares were sold to investors at $83 each. They opened at $111.50 and closed the first day at $97.17, which was 17% higher than the sale price. That made the company worth about $1.8 trillion.
On Friday the shares fell about 8.5% to $88.91, as investors worried about AI shares in general. CNBC said Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in total, though other reports give other totals.
It was a bad week for tech. Nvidia, the chipmaker, lost 23% of its value. The Nasdaq index fell about 10%, its worst week since 2020.
levels.why: Investors are asking whether AI companies are worth so much money.

levels.headline: Anthropic joins the stock market, but its shares slip
levels.body:
Anthropic is a company that makes the AI assistant Claude. On Thursday its shares went on sale to the public on the Nasdaq stock exchange, under the code ANT. The first price was $83. By the end of the first day, the price was $97.17, which was 17% higher. That valued the whole company at around $1.8 trillion.
But on Friday the price fell by about 8.5% to $88.91. Many investors were nervous about AI companies that week. CNBC said Anthropic raised about $93.5 billion in total, although other reports give different amounts.
The whole tech market had a bad week. The chipmaker Nvidia lost 23% of its value, and the Nasdaq fell about 10%.
levels.why: It shows how nervous investors are about the AI boom.

levels.headline: Anthropic's shares start trading and then slip
levels.body:
Anthropic is the company behind the AI assistant Claude. On Thursday, it began selling shares to the public on the Nasdaq stock exchange, with the code ANT. The first price was $83. By the end of the first day, it was $97.17, which is 17% higher. That valued the company at around $1.8 trillion.
On Friday the price fell about 8.5% to $88.91, as many investors felt nervous about AI companies. CNBC said Anthropic raised about $93.5 billion in total, though other reports give different figures.
The whole technology market had a bad week. The chipmaker Nvidia lost 23% of its value, and the Nasdaq fell about 10%. Anthropic's launch could not stop the fall.
levels.why: It shows how nervous investors are about the AI boom.

levels.headline: Anthropic's shares start trading, then fall
levels.body:
A company can sell small pieces of itself, called shares, to the public. The first time it does this is called an IPO. On Thursday, the AI company Anthropic did this on the Nasdaq stock exchange. Its code is ANT. The first price was $83. At the end of the first day it was $97.17. That made the company worth about $1.8 trillion.
On Friday the price fell about 8.5% to $88.91. That is still above the first price of $83. CNBC said the company raised about $93.5 billion by selling shares.
It was a bad week for tech companies in general. The chipmaker Nvidia lost 23% of its value in one week. The Nasdaq, which lists many tech firms, fell about 10%.
levels.why: It shows how much money is being put into AI.

levels.headline: Anthropic's shares start trading, then fall
levels.body:
Anthropic is a company that makes the AI helper called Claude. Last week it did something big. It sold small pieces of itself, called shares, to anyone who wanted to buy them. This is called an IPO. It happened on a stock exchange called the Nasdaq.
The first price was $83 a share. At the end of the first day it was $97.17. That made the whole company worth about $1.8 trillion. That is an enormous amount of money. But on Friday the price fell to $88.91.
It was a bad week for tech firms in general. Another big company called Nvidia lost nearly a quarter of its value. Many investors were nervous that AI firms might be worth less than people hoped.
levels.why: It shows how much people are betting on AI, and how risky that can be.

levels.headline: A big AI company sells shares, and the price wobbles
levels.body:
Anthropic is a company that makes an AI helper called Claude. Last week, it let people buy tiny parts of the company. These parts are called shares. A share costs money. It can go up or down. The first price was $83. After one day, it was $97.17, which was higher. So people who bought early were happy at first.
Then on Friday, the price dropped to $88.91. That was lower, but still more than the first price.
Other tech companies had a bad week too. One of them, Nvidia, lost nearly a quarter of its value. Many grown-ups are now nervous. They worry that AI companies might not be worth as much as they hoped.
levels.why: It shows how much money grown-ups are putting into AI.

levels.headline: A new company joins the share market, and its price goes up and down
levels.body:
Think about a lemonade stand. You let people buy a small piece of your stand for a few coins. If the stand does well, the piece is worth more. If it does badly, it is worth less. Those pieces are called shares.
Last week, a company called Anthropic did this, but on a giant scale. It makes an AI helper called Claude. The first share cost $83. After one day it was $97.17. Then on Friday it dropped to $88.91.
Other technology companies had a bad week too. Some lost lots of value. Grown-ups got nervous and asked, are these companies really worth that much? Nobody knows for sure yet.
levels.why: It shows that prices can go up and down quickly.

levels.headline: A computer company sells tiny pieces of itself
levels.body:
Imagine you bake a huge cake and cut it into tiny slices. You sell each slice for a few coins. A person who buys a slice owns a little bit of your cake. The slices are called shares.
Last week, a company called Anthropic did this. It makes a clever computer helper called Claude. People bought lots of slices. On the first day, each slice cost more than at the start. But on Friday, the price of a slice went down a bit.
Other computer companies had a bad week too. Their slices got cheaper. Grown-ups worry that the cake might not be worth as much as they hoped. For now, nobody knows what will happen next.
levels.why: It shows that prices can change quickly, so grown-ups must be careful.

headline: Traders price a December Federal Reserve rate hike as 10-year yield falls to about 4.93% on safe-haven buying

terms.meaning: The US central bank, which sets the main US interest rate.
One hundredth of a percentage point.
An asset investors buy when markets are nervous because it is expected to hold its value.

levels.headline: Traders price a December Federal Reserve rate hike as 10-year yield falls to about 4.93% on safe-haven buying
levels.body:
Markets are pricing in a quarter-point Federal Reserve interest rate rise in December, with CNBC reporting odds between about 92% and 100% and a small chance of a half-point move. October consumer prices rose 0.4% on the month, above forecasts.
On Friday 20 November, as shares sold off, investors moved into government bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 12 basis points to roughly 4.93%, after trading above 5% earlier in the week. The 2-year yield fell to about 4.63%.
St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has said the Fed may need as many as four more rises, and governor Christopher Waller has argued a bigger move may be needed. Minutes from the October meeting showed policymakers largely expected further increases but wanted more data. CNBC noted that reported odds vary by outlet and by day.
levels.why: Why it matters: higher US interest rates push up borrowing costs worldwide and can weigh on share prices.

levels.headline: A US interest rate rise looks likely in December as bond yields drop on Friday
levels.body:
Traders now see a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate rise in December as very likely. CNBC cited odds of 92% to 100%, with a small chance of a half-point rise. US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists had forecast.
On Friday 20 November, investors bought government bonds as shares fell. That pulled the 10-year Treasury yield down by around 12 basis points to about 4.93%, having been above 5% earlier in the week. The 2-year yield dropped to roughly 4.63%.
St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem said as many as four more rises may be needed. Governor Christopher Waller has said a larger move could be justified. Minutes of the October meeting showed officials expected more rises but wanted more data first.
levels.why: It affects the cost of borrowing in the US and around the world.

levels.headline: Markets expect the US central bank to raise interest rates again in December
levels.body:
Investors think the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, will raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point in December. CNBC put the odds at about 92% to 100%. US prices rose 0.4% in October, which was more than expected, and that is making officials worried about inflation.
On Friday 20 November, share prices fell and investors moved money into US government bonds, which are seen as safer. That pushed down the yield, the return on a bond, on the 10-year bond to about 4.93%. It had been above 5% earlier in the week.
One Fed official said as many as four more rises might be needed. Another said a bigger rise could be needed in December.
levels.why: It can make borrowing dearer and shares less attractive.

levels.headline: US interest rates look set to rise again
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. It sets the main interest rate, the price of borrowing money. Investors now think it will raise that rate by a quarter of a percentage point in December. CNBC says the chance is somewhere between 92% and 100%.
The reason is rising prices. US prices went up 0.4% in October, more than experts expected. When prices rise fast, central banks often raise rates to cool things down.
On Friday, share prices fell and many investors bought US government bonds, which are seen as safe. That made the return on those bonds, called the yield, drop to about 4.93%. One Fed official said as many as four more rises might be needed.

levels.headline: The US central bank looks set to raise interest rates again
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, and it sets the main interest rate. Investors now think it will raise that rate by a quarter of a percentage point in December. CNBC puts the chance at roughly 92% to 100%.
The reason is rising prices. US prices rose 0.4% in October, faster than experts expected. When prices rise quickly, central banks often raise rates to cool things down.
