levels.headline: The US central bank may raise interest rates again
levels.body:
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It decides the main interest rate. An interest rate is the price you pay for borrowing money. Investors now think the bank will raise the rate by a small amount in December. They think it is almost certain.
The reason is that prices in the US went up faster than expected in October. By 0.4% in one month. When prices rise too quickly, the bank raises rates to slow them down.
On Friday, share prices fell. Many investors moved their money into US government bonds, which are seen as safe. That pushed the return on the bonds down a little, to about 4.93%. One of the bank's officials said it might need to raise rates up to four more times.
levels.why: It can make loans cost more, in America and elsewhere.

levels.headline: America's big bank may make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
Every country has a special bank that looks after its money. In America it is called the Federal Reserve. It sets the interest rate. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. Right now, investors think the Fed will raise this rate in December.
Why? Prices in America went up faster than expected in October. When prices rise too fast, the Fed raises the rate. This makes people borrow less and spend less, so prices rise more slowly.
On Friday, share prices dropped. Many people put their money into government bonds instead. Bonds are a safe place to keep money. One Fed leader said they may need to raise rates up to four more times.
levels.why: It can change how much people pay on loans.

levels.headline: The money bank in America may charge more for loans
levels.body:
Lots of people borrow money. When you borrow, you pay back a bit extra. That extra bit is called interest. A big bank in America, called the Federal Reserve, decides how much extra people have to pay. Now it looks like it will raise the amount in December.
Why? Because prices in America have been rising quickly. Things in shops cost more than before. When the Fed makes borrowing cost more, people spend less, so prices stop climbing so fast.
On Friday, many people felt nervous about shares. They moved their money to something safer, called government bonds. One Fed leader said the bank might raise the amount four more times.
levels.why: It matters because many grown-ups borrow money.

levels.headline: A big bank may make borrowing more costly
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow a toy from a friend, and you promise to give back the toy plus one sweet as a thank you. That extra sweet is like interest. It is the extra you pay for borrowing.
A big bank in America, called the Federal Reserve, can decide how big the extra sweet should be. Right now, prices in America are going up quickly. So the bank is thinking about making the extra bigger. That would make people borrow less and buy less, and then prices would stop going up so fast.
Many grown-ups think this will happen in December. On Friday, some of them felt nervous and put their money somewhere safe.
levels.why: It affects how much grown-ups pay when they borrow money.

levels.headline: Why a faraway bank might make things cost more
levels.body:
Think about a big piggy bank for a whole country. In America, that special bank is called the Federal Reserve. It helps decide how much extra people pay when they borrow money. This extra is called interest.
Prices in America have gone up quickly. That means a sandwich or a toy costs more than before. To slow this down, the bank may make borrowing cost more. Then people will buy fewer things, and prices should stop climbing so fast.
Many grown-ups think this will happen in December. They felt a bit nervous on Friday, so some moved their money to safe places. It is a bit like putting your pocket money in a locked box.
levels.why: It can affect how much families pay for loans.

headline: Brent crude settles at $92.56 on Friday, down about 15% in a month but still 48% above a year ago

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
When more is supplied than is needed, which tends to push prices down.
The International Energy Agency, which advises countries on energy.

levels.headline: Brent crude settles at $92.56 on Friday, down about 15% in a month but still 48% above a year ago
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, rose 0.63% to $92.56 a barrel on Friday 20 November 2026, according to Trading Economics. Over the past month it has fallen 14.94%, but it remains 47.95% higher than a year earlier. Saturday and Sunday are non-trading days, so Friday is the latest price.
Other reports said Brent stayed near its lowest levels since late August and had fallen nearly 20% so far in November amid signs of recovering global supply. The International Energy Agency said the world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, and Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027.
CNBC reported that tanker disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz offset the surplus outlook on Thursday, leaving prices swinging between supply worries and expectations of oversupply.
levels.why: Why it matters: oil prices feed directly into petrol, diesel and heating costs and into inflation.

levels.headline: Oil ends the week near $92 a barrel after a sharp fall in November
levels.body:
Brent crude, the benchmark for international oil prices, rose 0.63% to $92.56 a barrel on Friday 20 November, according to Trading Economics. It is down almost 15% over a month but about 48% higher than a year ago.
Other reports said it stayed close to its lowest level since late August and had dropped nearly 20% so far in November as supplies recover. The International Energy Agency forecasts a surplus in the oil market in the fourth quarter of this year. Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027.
CNBC said that disruption to tankers near the Strait of Hormuz offset the surplus outlook on Thursday, so prices keep moving between fears of shortages and expectations of too much supply.
levels.why: It influences petrol prices, energy bills and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices are lower than a month ago but still high
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main international benchmark for oil, ended Friday at $92.56 a barrel, up 0.63% on the day. Over the past month it has fallen by nearly 15%. But it is still about 48% higher than a year ago. Markets are closed at weekends, so Friday is the latest price.
Other reports said oil is close to its lowest since late August, as supplies recover. The International Energy Agency, which advises governments on energy, says there will be more oil than the world needs by the end of the year. Goldman Sachs, a bank, expects an average price of $88 a barrel in 2027.
But trouble for tankers near the Strait of Hormuz keeps pushing prices up and down.
levels.why: Oil prices affect fuel costs and the price of many goods.

levels.headline: Oil costs less than last month, but still a lot more than last year
levels.body:
Oil is traded in barrels. The main international price, called Brent, ended Friday at $92.56 a barrel. That is a little up on Thursday. But over the past month it has gone down by almost 15%. It is still about 48% higher than a year ago. The markets are shut at weekends, so Friday is the latest price.
Oil prices have dropped because more oil is coming to the market. A group that advises countries on energy, the IEA, says there will be more oil than the world needs by the end of the year. A bank called Goldman Sachs thinks the price will be about $88 next year.
But problems for oil ships near the Strait of Hormuz can still push it up.
levels.why: Oil prices change how much we pay for petrol and gas.

levels.headline: Oil is cheaper than last month but costs more than last year
levels.body:
Oil is sold by the barrel. The main international price, called Brent, ended Friday at $92.56 a barrel. That is a little higher than on Thursday. But over the past month it has gone down by almost 15%. It is still about 48% higher than a year ago. Markets close at weekends, so Friday is the latest price.
Prices have fallen because more oil is coming to the market. An energy group, the IEA, says there will soon be more oil than the world needs. A bank called Goldman Sachs thinks the price will be about $88 next year.
But trouble for oil ships near the Strait of Hormuz can still push the price back up.
levels.why: Oil prices affect the cost of petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil is cheaper than last month but costs more than last year
levels.body:
Oil is sold by the barrel. The main world price, called Brent, ended Friday at $92.56 a barrel. A month ago it was about 15% higher. But it is still a lot more than a year ago, almost 48% more.
Why did it fall? More oil is arriving in the market. A group of energy experts, the IEA, thinks the world will soon have more oil than it needs. When there is plenty of something, the price usually falls. A bank called Goldman Sachs expects it to be about $88 next year.
But there is trouble for oil ships near a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. That can push prices back up.
levels.why: Oil prices help decide what we pay for petrol and heating.

levels.headline: The price of oil has gone down a bit but is still high
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid that comes from under the ground. It is used to make petrol for cars. It is sold by the barrel. A barrel of the main kind, called Brent, cost $92.56 on Friday. A month ago it cost about 15% more, so it has fallen. But it is still much more expensive than a year ago.
Why is it cheaper? More oil is coming to the market, and when there is lots of something, it costs less. Experts say there may soon be more oil than the world needs.
But trouble for ships in the Middle East can push the price up again. Everyone is watching to see what happens next.
levels.why: The price of oil changes how much petrol costs.

levels.headline: Oil is a little cheaper, but still costs a lot
levels.body:
Cars need petrol, and petrol is made from oil. When oil costs more, petrol often costs more too. A barrel of the main kind of oil cost $92.56 on Friday. A month ago it cost about 15% more, so the price has dropped a bit. But it is still much higher than a year ago.
The price fell because more oil is being made and sent around the world. When there is lots of something, the price goes down. It is a bit like when everyone has too many sweets, so they sell them cheaply.
But trouble for oil ships in the Middle East could push the price up again.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can help bring down the cost of petrol.

levels.headline: Why oil costs go up and down
levels.body:
Imagine your school has a tuck shop that sells sweets. If the shop gets lots of sweets, it can sell them for less. If the sweets run low, the price goes up. Oil works a bit like this. It is used to make petrol for cars.
A month ago oil was more expensive. Now there is more oil around, so the price has dropped a bit. It is still a lot more costly than last year, though.
But there is trouble for oil ships in a faraway sea. If ships cannot sail safely, there might be less oil to go round. Then the price could go up again. Grown-ups are watching the price very carefully.
levels.why: It matters because it affects what families pay for petrol.

levels.headline: Why petrol costs change
levels.body:
Think of petrol as a drink that cars need. It comes from oil. When there is plenty of oil, petrol can cost less. When oil is hard to get, petrol costs more.
A month ago oil was more expensive. Now there is more oil being sold, so the price has gone down a little. But it is still more costly than it was last year.
There is a worry too. Some oil ships travel through a place where there is a lot of trouble. If they cannot get through, there might be less oil. Then the price might go up. Grown-ups keep watching the price, because it changes what everyone pays.
levels.why: It affects the cost of petrol and the price of lots of things.

headline: COP31 climate talks run into overtime as fossil fuel language is dropped, then fought over

terms.meaning: The 31st annual United Nations climate conference, held in Antalya, Turkey.
Agreement by all countries, with no one blocking.
Money for poorer countries already hit by climate harm.

levels.headline: COP31 climate talks run into overtime as fossil fuel language is dropped, then fought over
levels.body:
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries were still struggling on Saturday 21 November 2026 to agree a deal at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, which was scheduled to end on Friday. The COP31 president said, "We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet."
A draft earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A second version published on Thursday removed every mention of them, which observers linked to opposition from Saudi Arabia and other big oil and gas producers. France, Panama and other countries signed a letter insisting on "a clear transition away from fossil fuels", and Panama threatened to block any consensus that fell short.
Finance for adaptation and for loss and damage is also disputed. The EU's top climate official said the summit would produce either a good deal or no deal. A new text was expected on Saturday, and I found no confirmation of a final outcome.
levels.why: Why it matters: the result shapes how fast the world moves away from the fuels that cause climate change.

levels.headline: COP31 climate summit overruns as countries fight over fossil fuels
levels.body:
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries were still trying to agree a deal on Saturday 21 November at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey. It was due to end on Friday. The summit's president said, "We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet."
An early draft called for fossil fuels to be phased out faster, but a second draft on Thursday removed all mention of them. Observers said Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers had opposed the wording. France, Panama and others wrote a letter demanding a clear transition away from fossil fuels, and Panama threatened to block agreement without it.
Money for poorer countries to adapt to climate change and to cover loss and damage is also disputed. A new text was expected on Saturday. No final result had been reported.
levels.why: The outcome will influence climate action for years.

levels.headline: Climate talks in Turkey go into extra time over fossil fuels
levels.body:
Nearly 200 countries are still trying to agree a deal at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. The talks were meant to finish on Friday 20 November but are still going. The summit's president said the talks were close to the finish line but not there yet.
An early draft said fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal should be phased out faster. A later draft dropped all mention of them, and observers said big oil producers such as Saudi Arabia did not want the wording. France, Panama and others said any deal must include a clear move away from fossil fuels. Panama said it might block an agreement without it.
The countries also disagree about money to help poorer nations. No final deal had been reported.
levels.why: Whether countries agree to cut fossil fuels will affect the climate.

levels.headline: World leaders are still arguing about oil, gas and coal at climate talks
levels.body:
Almost 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, in Turkey, for a big climate conference called COP31. It was due to end on Friday, but the talks are still going. The person in charge said they were close to the finish line, but not there yet.
The main argument is about fossil fuels, which are oil, gas and coal. One early plan said countries should stop using them faster. A later version left out any mention of them. Oil-producing countries such as Saudi Arabia are said to have pushed for that. Other countries, such as France and Panama, say the deal must include a clear plan to move away from fossil fuels.
They also disagree about money for poorer countries. No final deal had been reported.
levels.why: The decision affects how fast the world tackles climate change.

levels.headline: Climate talks run late as countries fight over oil, gas and coal
levels.body:
Countries from all over the world are at a big climate meeting in Turkey. It is called COP31. They want to agree a plan to slow down climate change. The meeting was meant to end on Friday. It is still going.
The big argument is about fossil fuels, which are oil, gas and coal. Burning them makes the Earth warmer. Some countries want a clear promise to stop using them. Other countries that make a lot of oil do not want that. One early plan had the promise. The next plan took it out. Some countries, including France and Panama, are very unhappy about that.
They also disagree about money to help poorer countries. No final deal had been reported.
levels.why: Climate decisions affect the weather and homes of people everywhere.

levels.headline: Climate talks run late as countries argue over oil, gas and coal
levels.body:
Almost 200 countries are at a big climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, called COP31. They want to agree a plan to slow down climate change. The meeting was due to end on Friday but is still going, and the person in charge says it is close to the finish line, but not there yet.
The main argument is about fossil fuels, which are oil, gas and coal. Burning them warms the Earth. Some countries want a clear promise to move away from them. Big oil producers such as Saudi Arabia are said to oppose that. France and Panama say the deal must include it, and Panama said it might block an agreement without it.
They also disagree about money to help poorer countries. No final deal had been reported.
levels.why: The result affects how fast the world tackles climate change.

levels.headline: Countries are still talking about how to protect the planet
levels.body:
Leaders from nearly 200 countries are at a big meeting in Turkey. They are trying to agree on how to slow down climate change. This is when the Earth gets warmer, mostly because people burn oil, gas and coal. The meeting was meant to finish on Friday, but it has gone on longer.
Some countries want a clear promise to stop using oil, gas and coal. Other countries that sell a lot of oil do not want to promise that. Both sides are still talking. They also need to agree about money to help poorer countries cope with floods and storms.
No final deal had been reported yet.
levels.why: It matters for the weather and homes of people everywhere.

levels.headline: Countries still cannot agree on how to look after the Earth
levels.body:
Nearly 200 countries are at a big meeting in Turkey. They are talking about how to stop the Earth getting too hot. This is called climate change. A lot of it is caused by burning oil, gas and coal.
The meeting should have finished on Friday, but the countries could not agree. Some want a clear promise to use less oil, gas and coal. Others sell lots of oil and do not want to promise that. They also talk about money to help poorer countries that have been hit by storms and floods.
The leaders have not reached a final deal yet. They are still trying.
levels.why: It matters for the weather and the planet we all share.

levels.headline: Countries are having a long meeting about keeping the Earth cool
levels.body:
Imagine a very long class meeting where everyone must agree before it can end. If one person says no, the meeting goes on. That is a bit like what is happening in Turkey.
Almost 200 countries are trying to agree how to stop the Earth getting too hot. A lot of the heat comes from burning oil, gas and coal. Some countries want a promise to burn less. Others sell lots of oil and do not want to promise. One small country said it would say no to any deal that was too weak.
They should have finished on Friday, but they are still talking.
levels.why: It matters for the planet where you live.

levels.headline: A long meeting about looking after the Earth
levels.body:
Imagine your class has to choose a rule, and everyone must say yes before you can go out to play. Some children want one rule, and some want a different one. So you all stay inside for longer.
That is a bit like a big meeting in Turkey now. Nearly 200 countries are trying to agree how to stop the Earth getting too hot. The heat comes from burning things like oil, gas and coal. Some countries want to burn less. Others sell lots of oil and are not so sure.
The meeting should have ended on Friday. The grown-ups are still talking and trying to agree.
levels.why: It matters because the Earth is our home.

headline: Five EU countries plan Rwanda return hubs, but critics question whether the plan is legal

terms.meaning: A centre outside the EU where people refused asylum are sent.
A person who asks a country for protection because they fear harm at home.
Courts being free from political control.

levels.headline: Five EU countries plan Rwanda return hubs, but critics question whether the plan is legal
levels.body:
Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece have announced plans to send rejected asylum seekers to return hubs in Rwanda, Euronews reports. The first stage is expected in 2027 as a pilot, with the first hub holding around 100 people with no legal right to stay in the EU at any one time.
The plan is enabled by the EU's new return regulation, which says such deals can only be made with countries that respect human rights. Critics doubt Rwanda meets that test. One report notes it scored 0 out of 4 on judicial independence, raising questions about whether migrants could challenge their treatment in court. They also point to the UK precedent, where the Supreme Court blocked a UK-Rwanda deal over a real risk that refugees would be sent back to places they had fled.
Rwanda says human rights are respected and that an independent monitoring mechanism, to which the five countries have committed, will ensure it. Legal challenges before European courts are widely expected once deportations begin.
levels.why: Why it matters: it could set a model for how Europe handles asylum, and tests the limits of human rights law.

levels.headline: Five European countries want to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
levels.body:
Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece plan to set up return hubs in Rwanda for people whose asylum claims have been refused, Euronews says. The plan would begin in 2027 with a pilot, and the first hub would hold around 100 people at a time.
The plan relies on the EU's new return regulation, which says such deals must be with countries that respect human rights. Critics question whether Rwanda qualifies. It scored 0 out of 4 on judicial independence in one report. They also point to the UK, where the Supreme Court blocked a similar deal because of the risk that refugees would be sent back to danger.
Rwanda says it respects human rights and that an independent monitoring system will make sure of it. Legal challenges are expected.
levels.why: It tests how far Europe can go in sending asylum seekers abroad.

levels.headline: Five EU countries plan to send people refused asylum to Rwanda
levels.body:
Five European Union countries, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece, say they want to send people whose asylum claims were rejected to centres in Rwanda. Euronews reports that a trial is expected in 2027, starting with about 100 people at a time.
The plan uses new EU rules that allow such deals only with countries that respect human rights. Critics say Rwanda may not meet this test. One report gave it 0 out of 4 for independent courts. They also remind people that the UK Supreme Court blocked a similar UK plan, saying there was a real risk that refugees could be sent back to places where they were in danger.
Rwanda says rights are respected and that independent monitors will check. Lawyers expect court cases.
levels.why: It could change how Europe deals with migration.

levels.headline: Five European countries want to send some migrants to Rwanda
levels.body:
Five countries in the European Union plan to send people who have been told they cannot stay in Europe to Rwanda, a country in Africa. The countries are Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece. A first trial is expected in 2027 with about 100 people at one time.
The EU has new rules saying that such deals are only allowed with countries that respect human rights. Some people say Rwanda does not. One report said its courts are not independent of the government. The UK once tried a similar plan, but its top court stopped it because refugees could be sent back to danger.
Rwanda says it respects rights and that independent monitors will watch. Court cases are expected.
levels.why: It raises questions about fairness and the law.

levels.headline: Some European countries want to send migrants to Rwanda
levels.body:
Some people leave their countries because they are in danger. They ask other countries to let them stay. If a country says no, they are expected to go home. Five countries in Europe, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece, now want to send some of those people to Rwanda, in Africa.
They would go to special centres there. A first trial is planned for 2027, with about 100 people at a time. Some people say this is wrong. They say Rwanda does not have courts that are free from the government, so people could not argue for their rights. The UK tried a similar plan, but its top court stopped it.
Rwanda says it treats people fairly.
levels.why: It affects people's rights and how countries decide who can stay.

levels.headline: Five European countries plan to send some migrants to Rwanda
levels.body:
Five countries in the European Union, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece, want to send people whose requests to stay in Europe have been refused to centres in Rwanda, a country in Africa. A first trial is planned for 2027 with about 100 people at a time.
EU rules say such deals can only be made with countries that respect human rights. Critics say Rwanda may not, and one report said its courts are not independent. They add that the UK's top court blocked a similar UK plan because refugees could be sent back to danger.
Rwanda says it respects rights and that independent monitors will check what happens. The plan is likely to face challenges in court, and lawyers say its legality is not yet settled.
levels.why: It raises questions about fairness and the law.

levels.headline: Five countries want to send some people to Rwanda
levels.body:
Some people leave their homes because they are in danger. They ask another country if they can stay. Sometimes the answer is no. Five countries in Europe, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece, say they want to send people who got the answer no to a country in Africa called Rwanda.
They plan to start in 2027 with about 100 people at a time. Many people say it is not fair. They worry Rwanda might not treat people well, or let them tell a judge their side of the story. The UK once tried the same idea, but a court said no.
Rwanda says it will treat everyone fairly. Lawyers think there will be court cases.
levels.why: It matters because it is about fairness for people in need.

levels.headline: A plan to move some people to another country
levels.body:
Some people leave their homes because it is unsafe. They ask another country if they can live there. Sometimes the answer is no. Five countries in Europe have a new plan for people who hear no. They want to send them to another country called Rwanda.
They would start in 2027, with about 100 people. Some people say this is not fair. They worry that people might not be treated well in Rwanda. A country called the UK tried a similar plan once, but a court said it could not go ahead.
Rwanda says it will treat everyone fairly. Lawyers think there will be arguments in court.
levels.why: It matters because everyone should be treated fairly.

levels.headline: Some countries make a plan to send people far away
levels.body:
Imagine a new child wants to join your school, but the school says there is no room. In this story, some countries have a plan for people who hear no when they ask to stay. They want to send them to a faraway country called Rwanda.
The plan is meant to start in 2027. Some grown-ups think it is sensible. Others say it is unfair. They worry about whether people will be looked after properly, and whether they can tell a judge if something is wrong. Another country tried a similar plan once, but a court said no.
Now lawyers will argue about it.
levels.why: It matters because grown-ups want rules to be fair to everyone.

levels.headline: A big argument about where people can live
levels.body:
Imagine a new boy comes to your school, but the school says it is full. Some people think he should go to another school far away. Other people think that would be unfair, because he would not know anyone.
That is a bit like a plan by five countries in Europe. They want to send some people who asked to stay to a faraway country called Rwanda. It might start in 2027. Some grown-ups say it is sensible. Others worry that people will not be treated kindly.
A court in another country once said no to a plan like this. Lawyers will probably argue about it again.
levels.why: It matters because everyone deserves to be treated kindly.

headline: Mexico captures FBI most-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro' in Sinaloa, with violence following

terms.meaning: A criminal group that makes money mainly from illegal drugs.
A list of the US Federal Bureau of Investigation's most wanted fugitives.
Countries passing secret information to each other to catch criminals.

levels.headline: Mexico captures FBI most-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro' in Sinaloa, with violence following
levels.body:
Mexican forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro", on Friday 20 November 2026 in Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa. He was on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list and the US State Department had offered a reward of up to $5 million.
Mexico's Defence Ministry said special forces from the army and National Guard carried out the arrest, with coordination between US and Mexican intelligence agencies. Two other leaders of his organisation were also detained. The raid set off fighting. Cartel members set up flaming roadblocks, four Mexican soldiers died, and security forces killed seven attackers and arrested eight people.
US Ambassador Ronald Johnson said intelligence sharing between the two countries helped make the operation possible. Homeland Security Investigations called it a major blow to one of Mexico's most powerful cartel networks. Euronews links him to the Beltran Leyva organisation, and CNBC says his cousin, described as its second-in-command, was also arrested. Early details may change.
levels.why: Why it matters: it shows deepening US-Mexico cooperation against cartels, under pressure from President Trump.

levels.headline: Mexico arrests a top US-wanted cartel leader, and violence follows
levels.body:
Mexican forces arrested Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro", on 20 November 2026 in Guasave, Sinaloa. He was on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list, and the US had offered a reward of up to $5 million.
Mexico's Defence Ministry said army and National Guard special forces made the arrest with the help of US and Mexican intelligence. Two other leaders of his group were also held. The raid triggered fighting, with burning roadblocks set up by cartel members. Four Mexican soldiers died, seven attackers were killed and eight people were arrested.
US Ambassador Ronald Johnson said intelligence sharing helped make the operation possible. Euronews links the man to the Beltran Leyva organisation. Reports may change as the investigation continues.
levels.why: It shows how the US and Mexico work together against cartels.

levels.headline: A top cartel boss wanted by the US is captured in Mexico
levels.body:
Mexican special forces have captured a drug gang leader called Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro". It happened on 20 November in Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa. He was on the FBI's list of its ten most wanted people. The US had offered a reward of up to $5 million.
Mexico's army said US and Mexican spies shared information to help with the arrest. Two other gang leaders were also caught. The raid led to fighting. Gang members set up burning roadblocks. Four Mexican soldiers were killed. Security forces killed seven attackers and arrested eight people.
The US ambassador said sharing information helped. Reports may change as the investigation goes on.
levels.why: It shows how the US and Mexico are working together against drug gangs.

levels.headline: Mexico catches a drug gang leader the US wanted
levels.body:
Mexican soldiers have caught a man called Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, who is also known as "El Chapo Isidro". He is the leader of a drug gang. He was caught on 20 November in a town called Guasave, in a part of Mexico called Sinaloa. The FBI, the main police force of the US, had him on its list of ten most wanted people.
The US and Mexico shared secret information to help catch him. Two other gang leaders were also caught. But there was fighting when the soldiers arrived. Gang members set fire to roads. Four Mexican soldiers died.
The US ambassador said sharing information helped catch him.
levels.why: It shows two countries working together to fight crime.

levels.headline: A wanted gang leader is caught in Mexico
levels.body:
Soldiers in Mexico have caught a man who leads a drug gang. His name is Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, and he is also called "El Chapo Isidro". The soldiers caught him on 20 November in a town called Guasave. The FBI, a police force in the United States, had wanted to catch him for a long time. It had him on a list of its ten most wanted people.
The US and Mexico shared secret information to find him. Two other gang leaders were caught too. There was a lot of fighting. Gang members set roads on fire. Four soldiers died.
The US ambassador said sharing information was a big help.
levels.why: It shows countries can work together to stop crime.

levels.headline: A dangerous gang leader is caught
levels.body:
A drug gang is a group of people who sell illegal drugs and use violence. In Mexico, soldiers have caught the leader of one of them. His name is Fausto Isidro Meza Flores. Some people call him "El Chapo Isidro". The soldiers caught him on 20 November. He was on a police list in America of the ten most wanted people.
The police in Mexico and America shared secret information to find him. Two other leaders were also caught. When the soldiers came, the gang fought back. They set roads on fire. Sadly, four soldiers died. Seven gang members also died.
The US ambassador said it was a big help to share information.
levels.why: It shows police in different countries can work together.

levels.headline: Soldiers catch a gang leader in Mexico
levels.body:
Mexico is a country next to the United States. Some people there are in gangs that sell illegal drugs. This week, soldiers caught a gang leader called Fausto Isidro Meza Flores. People also call him "El Chapo Isidro". Police in America wanted him too. He was on their list of the ten most wanted people.
The police in the two countries shared secret information. That helped the soldiers find him. Two more gang leaders were also caught. There was a fight, and the gang set roads on fire. Four soldiers died.
Grown-ups say this was a big step against gangs, though the danger is not over.
levels.why: It matters because police in two countries worked together.

levels.headline: A bad gang leader has been caught
levels.body:
A gang is a group of people who do bad things. Some gangs sell drugs, which are dangerous. In Mexico, soldiers have caught the leader of one gang. His name is Fausto Isidro Meza Flores. Police in another country, America, had been trying to catch him as well. He was on their list of the ten most wanted people.
The police in both countries shared secret clues. That helped the soldiers find him. Two other gang leaders were caught too. There was a fight, and sadly some soldiers died.
Grown-ups say this is a big step. But they know there is still a lot of work to do to keep people safe.
levels.why: It matters because police from two countries worked together to keep people safe.

levels.headline: Police catch a bad leader
levels.body:
Imagine a bully who is in charge of a gang at school. Everyone is afraid of him. One day, the teachers from two schools work together. They share clues and find him. They catch him.
Something like this has happened in Mexico. A gang leader who sells dangerous drugs has been caught by soldiers. Police in America had been looking for him too. The two countries shared clues. Two more gang leaders were caught as well. There was a fight, and sadly some soldiers died.
Grown-ups say it is a big step. But they know there is still a lot of work to do.
levels.why: It matters because people want to stay safe.

levels.headline: Good people catch a bad person
levels.body:
Imagine some children are being very unkind in the playground. They scare other children. The teachers from two schools talk to each other and share clues. Then they catch the unkind leader.
Something like that happened in Mexico. A leader of a dangerous gang was caught by soldiers. Police in America, a nearby country, helped by sharing clues. Two more gang leaders were caught too. But there was a fight, and sadly some soldiers died.
Grown-ups say it is good that he was caught. But there is still lots of work to do to keep everyone safe.
levels.why: It matters because everyone should feel safe.

headline: Representation of the People Bill in Lords committee: votes at 16 and a £100,000 cap on overseas donations proposed

terms.meaning: The step where a bill is examined line by line and amendments are proposed.
British citizens living abroad who are registered to vote in UK elections.
The rules on how parties and campaigners raise and spend money.

levels.headline: Representation of the People Bill in Lords committee: votes at 16 and a £100,000 cap on overseas donations proposed
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has reached its committee stage in the House of Lords, according to a government blog published on 2 November 2026. The bill would give 16 and 17-year-olds a say in elections for the first time. I did not find results of any Lords votes on the proposal.
Government policy summaries say the bill would cap donations from overseas electors at £100,000 a year, with a minimum residency period of one full calendar year for anyone returning to the UK from abroad. The government says the cap would apply retrospectively from the date it was announced, to stop donors rushing in large sums.
Other political finance measures include a ban on crypto donations, a company donation test based on post-tax profits, and stricter know-your-donor checks for donations above £11,180. The measures follow the Rycroft Review into foreign financial influence in UK politics. These are government proposals, and amendments in the Lords could change them.
levels.why: Why it matters: it would change who can vote and how UK politics is funded.

levels.headline: Lords examine bill that would give 16-year-olds the vote and limit overseas donations
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has entered committee stage in the House of Lords, according to a government blog from 2 November. The bill would give 16 and 17-year-olds a vote for the first time. No results of Lords votes on this were found.
Government summaries say overseas electors would be limited to donating £100,000 a year, and people returning from abroad would need a full calendar year of residency first. The government says this applies retrospectively from the date of the announcement, to stop a rush of donations.
The bill would also ban crypto donations, test company donations against post-tax profits, and tighten checks on donations above £11,180. It follows the Rycroft Review into foreign interference. These are proposals, and peers may amend them.
levels.why: It affects who gets a say and who can fund political parties.

levels.headline: A bill to lower the voting age to 16 and tighten party funding is in the Lords
levels.body:
A government bill called the Representation of the People Bill is now being examined in the House of Lords. A government blog from 2 November says it would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote for the first time. I could not find the results of any votes on this in the Lords.
The government also wants to limit donations from British people living abroad to £100,000 a year. People who return to live in the UK would need a full calendar year of living here first. The government says the cap would apply from the date it was announced, so donors cannot rush in big gifts.
Other plans include banning crypto donations and tighter checks on donors. These are proposals, and the Lords may change them.
levels.why: It could change who votes and how parties get money.

levels.headline: Lords examine plans to give 16-year-olds the vote
levels.body:
A new law is being discussed in the House of Lords. It is called the Representation of the People Bill. A government blog says it would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote for the first time. I could not find how the Lords voted on that part.
The bill also deals with money in politics. British citizens who live abroad could give a party no more than £100,000 a year. Someone coming back to the UK would have to live here for a whole year before giving large sums. The government says this stops people rushing to give money before the rule starts.
The bill would also ban donations in cryptocurrency and make parties check who donors are. The Lords can still suggest changes.
levels.why: It could change who gets a vote and how parties are funded.

levels.headline: A plan to let 16-year-olds vote is being discussed in the Lords
levels.body:
The UK has a group of people called the House of Lords. They look closely at new laws before they are agreed. Right now they are looking at a law called the Representation of the People Bill. The government says it would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote for the first time. I could not find how the Lords voted on this.
The bill is also about money for political parties. People who live abroad could give a party only £100,000 a year. The government says this protects elections from unfair influence. The bill would also ban donations made in digital money called crypto.
The Lords can still suggest changes before the bill becomes law.
levels.why: It could mean teenagers get a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: A new law could let 16-year-olds vote
levels.body:
In the UK, a vote helps choose who runs the country. At the moment, you must be 18 to vote in most elections. A new law, called the Representation of the People Bill, could let 16 and 17-year-olds vote too. The law is being looked at by a group of people called the House of Lords. I could not find how they voted.
The law is also about money for political parties. Parties need money to run. The new law would limit how much people living abroad can give. It would also stop gifts in digital money called crypto.
The Lords can still suggest changes before it becomes law.
levels.why: It could give teenagers a say in how the country is run.

levels.headline: A new law could let young people vote
levels.body:
In the UK, adults vote to choose who runs the country. Right now, you have to be 18 to vote in most elections. A new law could let 16 and 17-year-olds vote too. It is being looked at by a group of people called the House of Lords. I could not find how they voted yet.
The law is also about money. Political parties need money to run. The new law would limit how much people living in other countries can give. The idea is to stop people from far away having too much say.
The Lords can still change the law before it is finished.
levels.why: It could give teenagers a say about who runs the country.

levels.headline: Teenagers might get to vote
levels.body:
When grown-ups vote, they choose who runs the country. Right now you have to be 18 to vote in most elections. But a new law could let 16 and 17-year-olds vote too. Some important people in a group called the House of Lords are looking at the law now. They can suggest changes.
The law is also about money. Political groups need money, and some people give them gifts. The law would stop people living far away from giving too much. It would also stop gifts in a kind of digital money.
The law is not finished yet.
levels.why: It could mean young people get a say in choosing leaders.

levels.headline: A new rule might let teenagers vote
levels.body:
Imagine your class picks a leader by voting. Now imagine only the oldest children are allowed to vote. A new rule could let younger children join in too.
In the UK, grown-ups vote to pick who runs the country. At the moment you must be 18. A new law could let 16 and 17-year-olds vote too. A group of important people, called the House of Lords, are looking at it now. They might change it.
The new law is also about money that people give to political groups. It says that people far away should not be able to give too much.
levels.why: It could give young people a say.

levels.headline: Maybe older children will get to vote
levels.body:
Imagine your class picks a class helper by voting. But only the oldest children can vote. A new rule could let some younger children vote too.
In the UK, grown-ups vote to choose who runs the country. You have to be 18 right now. A new law could let teenagers aged 16 and 17 vote as well. Some important people, called the House of Lords, are looking at it now. They might change it.
The law would also say that people living far away cannot give too much money to the groups that want to run the country. It is meant to be fair.
levels.why: It could mean young people get to have their say.
